# MASTER
title: "Let Land Pay for the City"

abstract: |
  Cities in Africa and Asia will add about 2.5 billion people by 2050, and most of the roads, transit, water and drainage they will need is not yet built. Building it will raise the value of urban land by more than it costs, yet developing countries collect recurrent property taxes worth only a few tenths of a percent of GDP, against about 1 percent in advanced economies. This paper argues that land should pay for the city. A recurrent tax on land value, together with capture of the one-off rise in land value that new infrastructure creates, can fund a large share of urban infrastructure. Hong Kong and Singapore show the model at scale: public ownership of land and rail-plus-property development let mass transit pay much of its own way. A property tax that falls mainly on land is also a green tax. It rewards compact building, penalizes idle land on the urban fringe and makes transit viable, and the compact, walkable city it supports brings large health gains from fewer road deaths, cleaner air and more physical activity. The paper sets out how a poor city can adapt the model, the planning it needs, and a best-practice outline for a property tax and land value capture code.

# Land value is created by the public, so it is the natural base for public infrastructure {#sec-theory}

## Infrastructure raises land values, and the owner did nothing to earn the rise {.unnumbered}

The value of a plot of urban land is the capitalized value of what can be reached from it. A hectare beside a new metro station is worth more than the same hectare a day before the line opened, because the people who will live or work on it can now reach more jobs, customers and services in less time. The owner has not built anything. The public authority that built the line, and the other residents and firms whose presence makes access valuable, created the gain. Economists call the part of a return that requires no effort or investment from its recipient *economic rent*, and land value is the textbook case: the supply of land at a location is fixed, so its price is set entirely by demand, and demand is set by what the city around it provides.

The rise can be large compared with the cost of the infrastructure that causes it. A meta-analysis of 102 estimates from 23 studies finds that rail projects raise land and property values near stations, by amounts that vary widely with the type of rail, the market and the study design [@Mohammad2013]. When the uplift is summed over every plot within walking distance of every station, it often exceeds the construction cost of the line. That is why Hong Kong's rail operator can pay for much of its network from property development (@sec-hksg), and why a city that leaves the uplift with landowners pays for its infrastructure twice: once through the budget, and again through the higher rents that tenants pay landowners for the access the budget created.

The rise in land value is also the main way the benefits of urban infrastructure reach their final owners. Better roads, drainage and transit lower commuting costs and raise wages, but in a city where people can move, competition for the newly better locations bids those gains into rents and land prices [@ArnottStiglitz1979]. This *capitalization* is what makes land a good tax base for infrastructure. A tax on land value reaches the people who gain from the infrastructure, roughly in proportion to how much they gain, without the government having to measure each person's benefit.

## The Henry George theorem gives the theoretical limit {.unnumbered}

Under ideal conditions, the rents that a city's public goods create are exactly enough to pay for them. @ArnottStiglitz1979 showed that in a city of optimal size, aggregate differential land rents equal spending on pure local public goods. The result is called the Henry George theorem, after the nineteenth-century American who proposed that a single tax on land could replace all others. Its conditions are strict, and no real city meets them, but its message is practical. The infrastructure that makes a city productive creates a land-value base large enough to fund much of that infrastructure. A city that cannot finance its infrastructure while its land values soar has a tax design problem, not a resource problem.

## Two families of instruments capture land value {.unnumbered}

This paper uses *land value capture* to mean any public instrument that recovers for the public part of the land value that public action creates [@OECDLincoln2022]. The instruments fall into two families, which differ in timing and in what they need from the state.

*Recurrent taxes* are levied every year on the value of land, or of land and buildings together. They capture the uplift gradually, as values rise and are reassessed, and they give a steady revenue that can service debt. Their weakness is that they depend on a working valuation roll and on the political will to revalue.

*One-off capture instruments* recover the uplift at the moment it is created. The OECD and Lincoln Institute compendium of land value capture in 60 countries groups them into five types [@OECDLincoln2022]. An *infrastructure levy*, often called a betterment levy, is a one-time charge on the owners of land that benefits from a defined project, such as Colombia's *contribución de valorización*. A *developer obligation* requires a developer to provide or pay for the roads, schools or open space that a project needs as a condition of permission. A *charge for development rights* sells the right to build more floor area than the base zoning allows, as São Paulo does with its auctioned building-rights certificates. *Land readjustment* pools privately held plots, returns to the owners smaller but serviced and better-shaped plots, and keeps some land for roads and for sale, as in Japan and in the town planning schemes of Gujarat, India. *Strategic land management*, which includes public land leasing or sale, lets a government that owns the land sell or lease it after the infrastructure has raised its value, which is the core of the Hong Kong and Singapore models.

**Proposition 1 (land should pay).** *Where infrastructure raises land values, a combination of a recurrent land-value tax and one-off capture instruments can recover a large share of the infrastructure's cost from those who gain from it, at lower efficiency cost than taxes on labor, capital or consumption. The share recovered rises with the quality of the valuation roll and with the extent to which the public owns or controls the land before the infrastructure is announced.*

The second condition matters most in practice. Land prices move on the announcement of a project, not on its completion, so instruments that act after the announcement capture less of the uplift than instruments that act before it. A government that already owns the land, or that pools or acquires it at pre-project value, captures most of the gain. A government that relies on a recurrent tax with infrequent revaluation captures little of it for years.

## Land taxes are the least harmful taxes a government can levy {.unnumbered}

A tax on land value does not reduce the supply of land, so it does not shrink the economy the way taxes on work, saving or investment do. OECD research ranks recurrent taxes on immovable property as the least damaging to long-run growth, followed by consumption taxes, personal income taxes and, most damaging, corporate income taxes [@Johansson2008; @Arnold2011]. A tax on buildings is less benign than a tax on land, because buildings are produced and a tax on them discourages building. A tax on land alone, or a property tax with a lower rate on buildings than on land, keeps the growth advantage and adds the green advantages set out in @sec-green.


# Property taxes on land are green taxes {#sec-green}

A tax on land value is a green tax because it changes how land is used in the direction that lowers emissions and pollution. Green taxes are usually defined by their base: a tax on fuel, on carbon or on a pollutant. A land value tax has no environmental base, but it reshapes the city, and the shape of a city fixes how much its residents must travel, by what mode, and how much land, energy and materials each household uses for decades. Four mechanisms make the tax green.

## It pushes development inward and upward rather than outward {.unnumbered}

A land value tax raises the cost of holding valuable land idle or underused, which brings central and well-served land into use first. An owner of a vacant plot near a transit line pays the same land tax whether the plot is empty, holds a single-story shop or holds a ten-story apartment block. The tax is a fixed cost that the owner can only cover by using the land, so it rewards the most intensive use the zoning allows. A tax on buildings does the opposite, because every extra story raises the bill. The best available evidence comes from Pennsylvania, where some cities tax land at a higher rate than buildings. @BanzhafLavery2010 found that the split-rate tax raised the number of housing units built, through more units per building rather than larger homes, which is to say it raised density. @OatesSchwab1997 found that Pittsburgh's sharp shift toward land in 1979–80 was followed by a rise in building activity in the 1980s that fifteen comparable cities in the region did not share, while cautioning that a downtown redevelopment drive also played a part.

## It deters speculative land banking on the urban fringe {.unnumbered}

A land value tax makes it costly to hold land at the edge of a growing city in the hope of selling it later, which slows the leapfrog sprawl that characterizes fast-growing cities in developing countries. Without a holding cost, an owner of a peri-urban plot can wait for prices to rise, and development jumps past the withheld land to cheaper land further out. The city spreads, its infrastructure has to cover more distance per resident, and travel distances lengthen. A tax on the land's value, assessed at its value with planned infrastructure, makes waiting expensive. The design point is that agricultural land inside a planned urban extension should be valued at its urban-use value, or at least taxed on it, once infrastructure is committed. Many developing-country codes do the reverse and exempt agricultural land, which turns the urban fringe into a tax shelter for speculation.

## It funds transit and lets transit pay its way {.unnumbered}

Land value capture makes rail and bus rapid transit financially viable in places where fares alone cannot cover their costs, which tilts the choice between transit and roads toward transit. A road widening raises the value of the land along it much less than a metro station raises the value of land around it, because the station concentrates accessibility in a walkable radius. A city that captures land value therefore finds transit relatively cheaper than roads, while a city that relies on fuel taxes and general revenue sees no such signal. Hong Kong's rail network is the leading example (@sec-hksg).

## It replaces taxes that lock people in place {.unnumbered}

Shifting revenue from property transfer taxes to recurrent land taxes lets households move closer to work, which cuts commuting. Many developing countries raise more from stamp duties and registration fees on property sales than from recurrent property taxes (@sec-dev). A transfer tax is a fine on moving. In the United Kingdom, @HilberLyytikainen2017 found that the stamp duty reduced household mobility substantially, especially for short-distance moves that are about matching home to job. [VERIFY: exact magnitude.] Every extra kilometer a household commutes because it cannot afford to move adds to emissions, congestion and time lost. Transfer taxes also push transactions into informality, which keeps the land registry out of date and the valuation roll blind.

## The green effect needs planning to go with it {.unnumbered}

A land value tax supplies the incentive to build compactly, but planning has to permit it. If zoning caps building heights at two stories, minimum plot sizes are large and parking requirements absorb a third of each site, the tax cannot raise density; it can only raise revenue. The tax and the plan are complements. The plan sets where density is allowed and where infrastructure goes. The tax makes sure the allowed density is used and that the uplift funds the next round of infrastructure. @sec-green-model sets out the planning a poor city needs.

**Proposition 2 (property taxes on land are green taxes).** *A recurrent tax on land value, with buildings taxed at a lower rate or not at all, lowers the cost of compact development relative to dispersed development, raises the cost of holding serviced land idle, and gives transit a financing advantage over roads. Where planning permits higher density near transit, the tax lowers vehicle travel, energy use and emissions per resident. Where planning forbids density, the tax raises revenue but does not change urban form.*

The claim has limits that should be stated. The direct evidence on density comes mostly from rich-country cities, and the link from density to lower travel emissions is strong but not automatic: dense cities with poor transit still congest. The green case for the land tax is strongest as part of the package this paper describes, a land tax plus capture of transit uplift plus planning for density near transit, not as a stand-alone instrument.


# Best practice for a property tax and land value capture code {#sec-code}

A good fiscal code for land does four things. It defines a base that reaches land value and spares buildings. It requires a valuation roll that is complete, current and checked. It makes the tax hard to avoid and cheap to pay. And it gives the city legal tools to capture the uplift from infrastructure at the moment it is created. @tbl-code sets out the provisions; the paragraphs below explain the choices that matter most.

## Tax land more heavily than buildings, and move toward a pure land base over time {.unnumbered}

The code should define the base as the market value of land, or as the market value of land and buildings with a lower rate on the building component. A pure site-value base gives the strongest green and growth incentives and is simpler to value in fast-growing cities, where land transactions are frequent and buildings are often informal or unfinished. A split-rate base is the practical route where the existing roll values land and buildings together: the code fixes a ratio, such as a building rate one-quarter of the land rate, and narrows it on a published schedule. Annual rental value bases, common in South Asia and inherited from British rating, should be converted to capital value, because rental value understates the value of underused land and gives a vacant plot near zero liability.

## Value everything, often, by mass appraisal, and test the results in public {.unnumbered}

Valuation is where most developing-country property taxes fail, so the code should make it a legal duty with measurable standards. It should require a general revaluation at least every five years, with annual indexation between revaluations, so values never drift for decades. It should authorize computer-assisted mass appraisal from sales, rental and land-use data, and simpler banded or points-based methods where market data are thin, as Freetown adopted. It should require the valuation authority to publish annual ratio studies against the international standard of the International Association of Assessing Officers: a median ratio of assessed to market value between 0.90 and 1.10, and a coefficient of dispersion within set limits [@IAAO2013]. Publishing these statistics is the cheapest way to show taxpayers that the roll is fair, and the cheapest way to show the ministry where it is not.

## Put every parcel on the roll, whatever its legal status {.unnumbered}

The fiscal cadastre should cover every occupied parcel, whether or not it has a formal title, and the code should say plainly that being on the tax roll neither confers nor removes property rights. Separating fiscal registration from legal title removes the main excuse for leaving informal areas off the roll, and the main fear that keeps owners from registering. Satellite imagery and street-level surveys now make it possible to map every building in a city of several million in a year at modest cost. The code should place the duty to register on the occupier where the owner is unknown, and allow self-declaration of basic attributes, checked by sample audits.

## Keep exemptions few, explicit and costed {.unnumbered}

Exemptions should be limited to a small household allowance and to land used directly by government and recognized public-benefit bodies, and every exemption should be listed and costed each year. A basic allowance, a slice of land value exempt for every owner-occupied home, protects poor households better than a list of exempt categories and keeps the base broad [@StrettonWP21]. Blanket exemptions for agricultural land inside urban boundaries, for religious or political bodies' commercial property, and for new buildings for many years should be removed. Each one shrinks the base, and the agricultural exemption in particular rewards holding serviced land idle.

## Make collection easy and non-payment costly {.unnumbered}

The code should make unpaid tax a first charge on the property, so that it must be cleared before any sale, mortgage or building permit, and should authorize, as a last resort, the sale of the property to recover long-standing arrears. Payment by mobile money and bank transfer, bills delivered by text message, and interest on arrears set above the government's borrowing rate all raise compliance at low cost. Linking building permits, utility connections and business licenses to a clear tax account turns every interaction with the city into a collection point. Deferral for asset-rich, cash-poor households, such as elderly owners, can be offered with the tax accumulating as a charge settled on sale or inheritance.

## Let cities set rates within a national band, and let them keep the money {.unnumbered}

Rate-setting should sit with the city, within a minimum and maximum set in national law. The minimum stops a race to the bottom, and the maximum protects taxpayers. A city that sets its own rate and keeps the revenue is accountable to its own residents for both, which is the strongest political support a property tax can have. National transfers should not fall when a city collects more, or cities will stop trying. A vacant-land surcharge, a higher rate on serviced land left undeveloped for more than a set period, belongs in the code as an option for cities with fringe speculation.

## Give cities the legal tools to capture uplift before it is capitalized {.unnumbered}

The code should authorize the five land value capture instruments and set the procedures for each. For infrastructure levies, it should define a benefit zone around each project, a method for apportioning the charge, and payment over several years. For development rights, it should allow cities to sell floor area above a base ratio, by auction where demand is strong. For land readjustment, it should allow a majority of owners in a scheme area to proceed with compulsory participation of the minority, with clear rules for the share of land the authority keeps, as Gujarat's town planning law does. For public land, it should allow leasing with periodic rent review, so that the public owner shares in future increases in value, and require that proceeds from sales go to a capital fund rather than to current spending.

## Ring-fence the land revenues for capital, and publish what they buy {.unnumbered}

The code should send one-off capture revenues, which are lumpy and cyclical, to an urban infrastructure fund, and allow recurrent property tax revenue to service infrastructure debt. China's experience shows the danger of using land sales to fund current spending: when the property market turned, revenue that local governments had come to rely on fell sharply (@sec-dev). A fund that publishes each year what land revenue built, and where, gives taxpayers a reason to pay that a general budget cannot.

| Element | Best-practice provision | Common failure it avoids |
|---|---|---|
| Base | Market value of land; buildings at a lower rate or exempt; a path from rental to capital value | Annual-value bases that tax vacant land at near zero |
| Coverage | Every occupied parcel on the fiscal cadastre, regardless of title; registration does not confer or remove rights | Informal areas left off the roll |
| Valuation | General revaluation at least every five years; annual indexation; mass appraisal; published ratio studies against international standards | Rolls decades out of date; regressive assessment |
| Rates | Set by the city within a national minimum and maximum; optional vacant-land surcharge | Race to the bottom; speculative land banking |
| Exemptions | A basic household allowance; public land in public use; all exemptions listed and costed each year | Agricultural, religious and new-building exemptions that erode the base |
| Collection | Tax is a first charge on the property; mobile payment; interest above the borrowing rate; links to permits and utilities; deferral for cash-poor owners | Collection rates below half |
| Appeals | Independent, low-cost appeal with deadlines; tax payable pending appeal | Endless disputes that stall collection |
| Value capture | Infrastructure levies, developer obligations, sale of development rights, land readjustment, public land leasing with rent review | Uplift left with landowners |
| Use of revenue | Capture revenue to a capital fund; recurrent revenue may service infrastructure debt; annual public report | Land sales funding current spending |
| Transfer taxes | Cut stamp duties and registration fees as recurrent revenue rises | Taxes that freeze mobility and push sales off the record |

: Elements of a property tax and land value capture code. Source: author, drawing on @KellyWhiteAnand2020, @OECDLincoln2022 and @IAAO2013. {#tbl-code}


# The strongest objections, and the answers {#sec-risks}

## "The poor will lose their homes" {.unnumbered}

The most serious objection is that a land tax can force poor households off valuable land they occupy but cannot afford to be taxed on. A widow living in a family house in a district that a new metro has made valuable may own an asset worth a fortune and have no cash income. The answer lies in design. A basic household allowance exempts the land value of an ordinary home, so most poor households pay nothing [@StrettonWP21]. Deferral lets cash-poor owners accumulate the tax as a charge settled on sale or inheritance, so no one is forced to sell to pay it. And the alternative is not a world in which the poor keep their land. Without a property tax, the same metro raises rents for tenants, who are the poorest urban residents in most developing-country cities, while landlords keep the whole gain. A land tax with an allowance is more progressive than the status quo.

## "Informal tenure makes it impossible" {.unnumbered}

A second objection is that a property tax needs clear titles, and most land in many African and South Asian cities has none. The answer is that a tax roll needs an occupier and a value, not a title. Kampala, Freetown and many Indian cities tax properties without formal title, and doing so can strengthen tenure security in practice, because a tax receipt is evidence of occupation. The code should say explicitly that registration for tax does not confer or remove rights, which protects both the occupier and the state.

## "Land value capture fuels bubbles and debt" {.unnumbered}

A third objection is that dependence on land sales ties public finances to the property cycle, as China has shown. The objection is right about land sales and wrong about recurrent taxes. Revenue from selling land rises and falls with the market, and when it funds current spending or backs borrowing, a downturn becomes a fiscal crisis. A recurrent land tax is far more stable, because it is levied on the stock of land value rather than on the flow of transactions. The answer is to use one-off capture for capital spending only, to build up the recurrent tax as the main revenue, and to keep borrowing against future land sales within strict limits.

## "Compulsory acquisition and land pooling invite abuse" {.unnumbered}

A fourth objection is that the Singapore model rested on acquiring land at below-market prices, which few democracies would accept and which in weaker states becomes a license to evict the poor and enrich the connected. The objection is fair, and it is why this paper recommends land readjustment and land value taxes rather than compulsory acquisition as the main tools for most countries. Land readjustment leaves owners on their land, with a smaller but more valuable plot, and requires the consent of a majority. Where acquisition is used, the code should require market-value compensation, published valuations and independent appeal.

## "Cities lack the capacity" {.unnumbered}

A fifth objection is that the cities that most need this model have the least capacity to run it. That is true, but the capacity required has fallen sharply. Satellite imagery, cheap smartphones for field surveys, mobile money and open-source mass appraisal software have cut the cost of building and running a fiscal cadastre by an order of magnitude in two decades. The binding constraint is political, not technical: a mayor has to be willing to send bills to the city's most powerful landowners. National governments and development banks can help by financing the first valuation roll and by rewarding cities that raise their own revenue rather than penalizing them.
